content: Reinforcing the emphasis on anti-corruption, transparency, and accountability within national health policies, strategies, and plans is a critical step in strengthening health systems. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been actively working on these areas during the 2018–2019 biennium, as part of its broader efforts to support universal health coverage (UHC). This initiative is a collaborative effort involving WHO’s Health Systems Governance and Financing team, as well as the Gender, Equity, and Human Rights team, with contributions from external experts and partners. The WHO publication on this topic was developed through a cross-departmental technical collaboration, led by Theadora Swift Koller and David Clarke from WHO headquarters. The document was authored by Taryn Vian, a WHO consultant and professor at Boston University School of Public Health, with input from other experts. It was informed by discussions held during WHO technical meetings and workshops on anti-corruption, transparency, and accountability in health systems. Corruption in the health sector is a significant barrier to achieving UHC, as it leads to the loss of public funds, undermines evidence-based policymaking, and erodes trust in health systems. It is associated with negative health outcomes, including higher child mortality rates. Addressing corruption requires robust situation analysis and tailored interventions that consider the specific institutional, political, and contextual factors of each country. Transparency involves providing citizens with timely and reliable information about their rights, entitlements, and the decision-making processes of government officials. This includes the criteria and evidence used to make decisions. Transparency can deter corruption by exposing unethical practices to public scrutiny. Accountability requires institutions to explain their performance in achieving goals and addressing public needs. It also demands visible and responsive actions when standards and commitments are not met. When governance is transparent, and citizens are engaged in decision-making processes, public officials are more likely to be held accountable, reducing opportunities for corruption. Citizen participation is essential for ensuring that public decisions reflect the needs and priorities of the population. It enables individuals to share their views and influence governance processes. Together, transparency, accountability, and citizen participation create an environment where corruption is less likely to thrive. The WHO publication provides detailed recommendations for integrating anti-corruption, transparency, and accountability into the development of national health policies, strategies, and plans (NHPSPs). These efforts aim to support WHO Member States in preventing corruption and strengthening their health systems through greater transparency and reinforced accountability mechanisms.
